Small rooms suffer from bass booms and large seat-to-seat differences. Bass traps, the proven remedy, are big and must sit in specific spots, often where windows or doors are. Floyd Toole, whose bass-trapped lab at the National Research Council of Canada became the prototype for the IEC 268-13 listening room, recounts how his own homes pushed him toward alternatives.

Around 1988 he tamed a booming home theater by placing in-phase subwoofers in opposite-polarity lobes of the offending modes, which he presented in 1990 as, to his knowledge, the first use of multiple subwoofers against room modes. In a 7,770 ft³ music room with a 42 Hz mode, a parametric EQ matched to the resonance’s frequency and Q worked as well as moving his chair: low-frequency room resonances are minimum-phase, so correct EQ fixes both magnitude and ringing. Either way, the modes return once the system is off.

At Harman, Todd Welti simulated up to 5,000 subwoofers (“acoustic wallpaper”) and showed that four, or even two, well placed give consistent bass at central seats in rectangular rooms. Welti and Allan Devantier then developed Sound Field Management, which measures every subwoofer at every seat and sets gain, delay and a parametric filter for each to minimize seat-to-seat variation. Toole also warns that waterfall plots trade frequency resolution against time resolution, and that bass traps remain the answer for studios and performance spaces.

A short preface by Fanyu Meng points out the room-acoustics basics behind the story: modes, interference, minimum-phase systems and EQ.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “History of Multi-Sub & Sound Field Management (SFM) for Small Room Acoustics” by Floyd Toole, published on Audioholics. Read the original.
